content: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has been shown to be effective in addressing antisocial behavior in both adolescents and adults. However, treating antisocial behavior in youth within residential settings presents unique challenges. These settings often involve individuals with more severe behavioral issues, and the closed environment limits opportunities to sustain behavioral changes after release. Additionally, the motivation for change among these youths is typically low. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of CBT in reducing recidivism among adolescents placed in secure or non-secure residential facilities. A secondary aim was to determine whether interventions targeting specific criminogenic needs are more effective than those with a broader focus on cognition and behavior. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Sociological Abstracts, ERIC, and Dissertation Abstracts International, covering studies from the 1960s to 2005. Experts in the field were also consulted to identify ongoing research. The inclusion criteria required studies to involve young people aged 12 to 22 who were placed in residential settings due to antisocial behavior. Both randomized controlled trials and studies with non-randomized comparison groups were considered. Two independent reviewers screened 93 titles and abstracts, ultimately retrieving 35 full-text reports. Data from 12 eligible trials were extracted and analyzed using RevMan software. Due to significant variability among the included studies, a random-effects model was employed for data synthesis. Results were reported at 6, 12, and 24 months post-treatment and were presented in forest plots. Odds ratios were used to measure outcomes, and intention-to-treat analyses accounted for dropouts. Pooled estimates were weighted using inverse variance methods, with 95% confidence intervals applied. The findings at the 12-month follow-up indicated that while individual studies often showed no significant effects, the pooled data demonstrated a statistically significant benefit of CBT compared to standard treatment. The odds ratio was 0.69, suggesting an approximate 10% reduction in recidivism on average. However, no significant effects were observed at the 6-month or 24-month follow-ups, nor when CBT was compared to alternative treatments. In conclusion, CBT appears to be slightly more effective than standard treatment for reducing recidivism among youth in residential settings. The benefits become evident around one year after release. However, there is no evidence to suggest that these effects persist in the long term or that CBT is superior to other alternative treatment approaches.
